title: The degree-two homogeneous perturbation conjecture for polynomial automorphisms

$$

title: Rudin's conjecture
literal_statement:
For positive integers $N,q,a$, let

$$
Q(N;q,a)=\#\{\,n\in\mathbb{Z}: 0\le n\le N-1,\ qn+a \text{ is a perfect square}\,\},
$$

that is, the number of perfect squares among the $N$ terms $a,\ q+a,\ 2q+a,\
\ldots,\ (N-1)q+a$ of the arithmetic progression $qn+a$, and set

$$
Q(N)=\max\{\,Q(N;q,a): q\ge 1,\ a\ge 1\,\}.
$$

Then:

1. $Q(N)=O\!\left(\sqrt{N}\right)$, i.e. there is an absolute constant $C>0$
with $Q(N)\le C\sqrt{N}$ for every positive integer $N$.

2. (Strong form) For every integer $N>6$,

$$
Q(N)=Q(N;24,1),
$$

so that the maximum number of squares in an
$N$-term arithmetic progression is attained by the progression $24n+1$, whose
terms $24n+1$ are squares exactly when $n$ is a generalized pentagonal number.

3. (Super-strong form) If $N=GP_k+1\ge 8$, where $GP_k$ denotes the $k$-th
generalized pentagonal number, then the progression
$24n+1$ is, up to equivalence, the only arithmetic progression of length $N$
with $Q(N;q,a)=Q(N)$; here two progressions $qn+a$ and $q'n+a'$ of length $N$
are equivalent when one is obtained from the other by a common square factor,
i.e. $(q',a')=(d^2q,d^2a)$ for some positive integer $d$, and by reversing the
order of the $N$ terms.
technical_disposition: Three scopes: O(sqrt N), exact maximization by 24n+1 for every N>6, and uniqueness up to the stated equivalence at pentagonal endpoints. title: covering problem of Rado
literal_statement:
For a finite family $\mathcal{S}$ of squares in the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, all of
whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axes and whose side lengths may
differ, write

$$
|\mathcal{S}| = \operatorname{area}\Big(\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal{S}} S\Big).
$$

Call a subfamily
$\mathcal{I}\subseteq\mathcal{S}$ independent if the squares belonging to $\mathcal{I}$
are pairwise disjoint; for such a subfamily $|\mathcal{I}|$ is the sum of the
areas of its members. Put

$$
F=\inf_{\mathcal{S}}\ \sup_{\mathcal{I}}\ \frac{|\mathcal{I}|}{|\mathcal{S}|},
$$

where
$\mathcal{S}$ ranges over all finite families of axis-parallel squares with $|\mathcal{S}|>0$
and, for each such $\mathcal{S}$, the subfamily $\mathcal{I}$ ranges over all
independent subfamilies of $\mathcal{S}$.

Then

$$
F=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Equivalently: every finite family of axis-parallel squares in
$\mathbb{R}^2$ whose union has area $1$ contains a subfamily of pairwise
disjoint squares of total area at least $\tfrac14$, and the constant $\tfrac14$
is largest possible, i.e. for every
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite family of axis-parallel squares whose union has area $1$
in which every subfamily of pairwise disjoint squares has total area less than
$\tfrac14+\varepsilon$.

title: Erdős–Oler conjecture
literal_statement:
For an integer $n \ge 1$, call a family of $n$ closed disks of radius $1$ in the
Euclidean plane a *packing* of an equilateral triangle
$T$ if every disk is contained in $T$ and the disks have pairwise disjoint
interiors, and set

$$
s(n) = \min\{\, s > 0 : \text{some closed equilateral triangle of side } s \text{ admits a packing by } n \text{ unit disks} \,\},
$$

so that
$s(n)$ is the side length of the smallest equilateral triangle into which $n$
non-overlapping unit circles can be packed. (Equivalently, by scaling,
$1/s(n)$ is the largest $r$ such that $n$ non-overlapping disks of radius $r$
fit inside an equilateral triangle of side $1$.)

For every integer $k \ge 2$ and $n = \binom{k+1}{2} = \frac{k(k+1)}{2}$,

$$
s(n-1) = s(n).
$$

That is, for every triangular number $n$, an optimal packing of $n-1$ unit
circles is obtained by deleting a single circle from an optimal packing of
$n$ unit circles in the triangle of side $s(n)$.

title: disk covering problem
literal_statement:
For a point $c\in\mathbb{R}^2$ and $r>0$ write
$B(c,r)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:\lVert x-c\rVert\le r\}$, and let $D=B(0,1)$ be the
closed unit disk.

For each integer $n\ge 1$ put

$$
r(n)=\inf\Big\{\,r>0\;:\;\exists\,c_1,\dots,c_n\in\mathbb{R}^2 \text{ with } D\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}B(c_i,r)\,\Big\}.
$$

Determine $r(n)$ for every $n\ge
1$, together with centers $c_1,\dots,c_n\in\mathbb{R}^2$ for which

$$
D\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}B\big(c_i,r(n)\big),
$$

so that the infimum is attained.

$$
N(\varepsilon)=\min\Big\{\,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\;:\;\exists\,c_1,\dots,c_n\in\mathbb{R}^2 \text{ with } D\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}B(c_i,\varepsilon)\,\Big\},
$$

the least number of disks of radius $\varepsilon$ whose union contains $D$; here
$N(\varepsilon)=\min\{n\ge 1:r(n)\le\varepsilon\}$.

title: kissing number problem
literal_statement:
For an integer $d\ge 1$, call a finite set
$\{x_{1},\dots,x_{N}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ admissible if

$$
x_{n}^{\mathsf{T}}x_{n}=1\quad\text{for all }n,\qquad (x_{n}-x_{m})^{\mathsf{T}}(x_{n}-x_{m})\ge 1\quad\text{for all }m\neq n,
$$

that is, if the
$x_{n}$ are unit vectors whose pairwise angular separations are all at least $60^{\circ}$.
Let

$$
\tau_{d}=\max\{N\in\mathbb{N}: \text{there exists an admissible set of } N \text{ vectors in } \mathbb{R}^{d}\},
$$

which is finite by compactness of the unit sphere. Equivalently,
$\tau_{d}$ is the greatest number of closed balls of radius $1$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with pairwise disjoint interiors that can all be tangent to one fixed closed ball of radius $1$:
after translating the fixed ball to be centred at the origin and rescaling the
centres of the tangent balls by
$1/2$, tangency to the central ball becomes $\|x_{n}\|=1$ and disjointness of
interiors becomes $\|x_{n}-x_{m}\|\ge 1$.

Determine the value of $\tau_{d}$ for every integer $d\ge 1$.

title: Kobon triangle problem

the maximum being taken over all arrangements $\mathcal{A}$ of $k$ distinct
lines in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

Determine $N(k)$ as an explicit function of $k$ for every integer $k \ge 3$.

title: McMullen problem
literal_statement:
For an integer $d\ge 1$, a finite set of points in
$\mathbb{R}^d$ is said to be in general position if no $d+1$ of its points lie
in a common hyperplane, and in convex position if every one of its points is a
vertex of the convex hull of the set. A projective transformation of
$\mathbb{R}^d$ is a map of the form

$$
T(x)=\frac{Ax+b}{\langle c,x\rangle+\delta},\qquad \begin{pmatrix}A & b\\ c^{\mathsf T} & \delta\end{pmatrix}\in \mathrm{GL}_{d+1}(\mathbb{R}),\ A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d},\ b,c\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\ \delta\in\mathbb{R},
$$

defined at those $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ with $\langle c,x\rangle+\delta\neq 0$.

For $d\ge 2$ let $\nu(d)$ be the largest integer $N$ with the property that for
every set $X\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ of $N$ points in general position there exists
a projective transformation $T$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that is defined at every point
of $X$ and such that $T(X)$ is in convex position.

Then

$$
\nu(d)=2d+1\qquad\text{for every }d\ge 2;
$$

that is, for every $d\ge 2$ and every set of
$2d+1$ points in general position in $\mathbb{R}^d$ there is a projective
transformation, defined at all these points, carrying them onto the vertex set
of a convex polytope, whereas for each $d\ge 2$ there exists a set of
$2d+2$ points in general position in $\mathbb{R}^d$ admitting no such
transformation.

This needs a uniform oriented-matroid or hyperplane-separation argument in all dimensions. title: Orchard-planting problem
literal_statement:
Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer. For a finite set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ of
$n$ points, no line containing all of them, call a line $\ell \subset
\mathbb{R}^2$ a $3$-point line of $P$ if $|\ell \cap P| = 3$, and let $f(P)$
denote the number of $3$-point lines of $P$. Set

$$
t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n) \;=\; \max\bigl\{\, f(P) \;:\; P \subset \mathbb{R}^2,\ |P| = n,\ P \text{ not contained in a line} \,\bigr\}.
$$

Determine $t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n)$ by an explicit formula valid for every $n
\ge 3$, and determine all configurations $P$ with $|P| = n$ for which
$f(P) = t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n)$.

Here $P$ ranges over sets of $n$ distinct points, and lines meeting
$P$ in fewer than $3$ or more than $3$ points are not counted in $f(P)$. Since
two distinct lines meet $P$ in at most one common point, the counting bound

$$
t_3^{\text{orchard}}(n) \;\le\; \left\lfloor \binom{n}{2} \Big/ \binom{3}{2} \right\rfloor \;=\; \left\lfloor \frac{n^2 - n}{6} \right\rfloor
$$

holds for all such $n$.

title: Bellman's lost-in-a-forest problem
literal_statement:
Let $F \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2}$ be a closed set with nonempty interior (a
"forest"), given up to congruence, and let
$\mathrm{SE}(2)$ denote the group of orientation-preserving isometries of $\mathbb{R}^{2}$
(rotations and translations), each element of which encodes a possible starting
position and heading of a hiker.

A rectifiable curve $\gamma : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}^{2}$ is called an *escape
path* for $F$ if

$$
g(\gamma([0,1])) \not\subseteq \operatorname{int} F \qquad \text{for every } g \in \mathrm{SE}(2);
$$

equivalently, a hiker who walks the curve
$\gamma$ starting from any point of $\operatorname{int}
F$ with any heading necessarily meets $\partial
F$ at some moment, and no congruent (directly congruent) copy of $\gamma$ lies
entirely in $\operatorname{int} F$.

Writing $\operatorname{length}(\gamma)$ for the total length of $\gamma$, set

$$
e(F) \;=\; \inf \bigl\{ \operatorname{length}(\gamma) \;:\; \gamma \text{ is an escape path for } F \bigr\}.
$$

Determine $e(F)$, and exhibit a curve $\gamma$ attaining this infimum, for an
arbitrary forest $F$; in particular, do so for every convex $F \subseteq
\mathbb{R}^{2}$ with nonempty interior, bounded or unbounded.

title: Negami's conjecture
literal_statement:
All graphs are finite and undirected. For graphs $C$ and $H$, a covering map
from $C$ to $H$ is a surjection $f$ from the vertex set of $C$ onto the vertex
set of $H$ such that, for every vertex $v$ of $C$, $f$ restricts to a bijection
from the set of neighbors of $v$ in $C$ onto the set of neighbors of
$f(v)$ in $H$. If such an $f$ exists, $C$ is called a covering graph of
$H$; if in addition $C$ is planar, then $C$ is a planar cover of $H$. When
$H$ is connected, every vertex of $H$ has the same number of preimages under
$f$, and this number is the ply of the map.

For every connected graph $H$ that has a finite planar cover, $H$ embeds in the
projective plane.

Equivalently, for every connected graph
$H$ admitting a finite planar cover, the minimum ply of a planar cover of $H$ is
$1$ or $2$.

title: Degree diameter problem
literal_statement:
For a finite simple undirected graph $G$ let $|V(G)|$ denote its number of
vertices, $\Delta(G)$ its maximum degree, and $\operatorname{diam}(G)$ its
diameter (the maximum, over all pairs of vertices, of the length of a shortest
path joining them). For positive integers $d$ and $k$ set

$$
n_{d,k}=\max\bigl\{\,|V(G)| : G \text{ finite simple undirected},\ \Delta(G)\le d,\ \operatorname{diam}(G)\le k\,\bigr\},
$$

and let

$$
M_{d,k}=1+d\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(d-1)^{i}=\begin{cases}1+d\dfrac{(d-1)^{k}-1}{d-2}, & d>2,\\[6pt] 2k+1, & d=2,\end{cases}
$$

so that $n_{d,k}\le M_{d,k}$ for all $d,k\ge 1$, and $n_{d,1}=d+1$, $n_{1,k}=2$,
$n_{2,k}=2k+1$.

Determine $n_{d,k}$ for all integers $d,k\ge
2$. In particular, for every fixed integer $k\ge 2$,

$$
\lim_{d\to\infty}\frac{n_{d,k}}{d^{k}}=1,
$$

equivalently $n_{d,k}=(1-o(1))\,M_{d,k}$ as $d\to\infty$ with
$k$ fixed; that is, writing $\mu_{k}=\liminf_{d\to\infty}
n_{d,k}/d^{k}$, one has $\mu_{k}=1$ for every $k\ge 2$.

A graph $G$ with $\Delta(G)\le d$, $\operatorname{diam}(G)\le
k$ and $|V(G)|=M_{d,k}$ is a Moore graph; such a graph is necessarily
$d$-regular. There exists a Moore graph with $d=57$ and
$k=2$, i.e. a $57$-regular graph on $M_{57,2}=3250$ vertices of diameter $2$.

title: Gilbert–Pollak conjecture
literal_statement:
For a finite set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ with $|P|\ge
2$, and for any finite set $Q\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, let

$$
\mathrm{mst}(Q)=\min_{T}\ \sum_{\{u,v\}\in E(T)}\|u-v\|,
$$

the minimum being taken over all spanning trees
$T$ of the complete graph on the vertex set $Q$, where
$\|\cdot\|$ is the Euclidean norm; thus $\mathrm{mst}(P)$ is the length of a
Euclidean minimum spanning tree of
$P$. Define the length of a Steiner minimum tree of $P$ by

$$
\mathrm{smt}(P)=\inf\{\,\mathrm{mst}(P\cup S)\ :\ S\subset\mathbb{R}^2,\ S \text{ finite}\,\},
$$

the points of $S$ being the Steiner points. Then $\mathrm{smt}(P)\le
\mathrm{mst}(P)$ for every such $P$, and

$$
\mathrm{mst}(P)\ \le\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,\mathrm{smt}(P)
$$

for every finite $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ with $|P|\ge 2$. Consequently the
Steiner ratio of the Euclidean plane,

$$
\rho=\sup_{P}\ \frac{\mathrm{mst}(P)}{\mathrm{smt}(P)},
$$

the supremum being over all finite $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ with $|P|\ge
2$, equals $2/\sqrt{3}$; the value
$2/\sqrt{3}$ is achieved by the three vertices of an equilateral triangle of unit side length, for which $\mathrm{mst}(P)=2$
and $\mathrm{smt}(P)=\sqrt{3}$, the Steiner point being the centroid of the
triangle.

title: Ryser's conjecture
literal_statement:
Let $r \ge 2$ be an integer and let $H = (V, E)$ be a hypergraph, i.e.
$V$ is a finite set and $E$ is a finite collection of subsets of $V$.

Say that $H$ is $r$-uniform if $|e| = r$ for every $e \in E$, and that
$H$ is $r$-partite if there is a partition $V = V_1 \cup \cdots \cup V_r$ into
pairwise disjoint sets such that $|e \cap V_i| = 1$ for every $e \in E$ and
every $i \in \{1, \dots, r\}$.

A matching in $H$ is a set $M \subseteq
E$ of pairwise disjoint hyperedges, and $\nu(H)$ denotes the maximum cardinality
of a matching in $H$. A transversal (vertex cover) in $H$ is a set
$T \subseteq V$ with $T \cap e \neq \emptyset$ for every $e \in E$, and
$\tau(H)$ denotes the minimum cardinality of a transversal in $H$.

Then for every integer $r \ge 2$ and every hypergraph
$H$ that is both $r$-uniform and $r$-partite,

$$
\tau(H) \le (r-1)\cdot \nu(H).
$$

title: Szemerédi's theorem
literal_statement:
For a subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, define its upper density by

$$
\limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{|A \cap \{1, 2, 3, \dotsc, n\}|}{n},
$$

and say that $A$ has positive upper density if this quantity is $>
0$. For an integer $k \geq 1$, an arithmetic progression of length $k$ is a set
of the form $\{a, a+d, a+2d, \dotsc, a+(k-1)d\}$ with $a, d$ positive integers.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ have positive upper density. Then for every
positive integer $k$, the set $A$ contains an arithmetic progression of length
$k$.

Equivalently, in finitary form: for every positive integer
$k$ and every real $\delta \in (0,1]$ there exists a positive integer $N_0 =
N_0(k,\delta)$ such that for every $N \geq N_0$, every subset of $\{1, 2,
\dotsc, N\}$ of size at least $\delta
N$ contains an arithmetic progression of length $k$. Writing
$r_k(N)$ for the largest cardinality of a subset of $\{1, 2, \dotsc,
N\}$ containing no arithmetic progression of length $k$, this asserts that for
every fixed $k$,

$$
r_k(N) = o(N) \qquad (N \to \infty).
$$

title: Piltz divisor problem
literal_statement:
For an integer $k\geq 2$ and a positive integer $n$, let

$$
d_{k}(n)=\#\{(n_{1},\dots ,n_{k})\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}^{k}\;:\;n_{1}n_{2}\cdots n_{k}=n\},
$$

so that $d_{2}(n)=d(n)=\sigma_{0}(n)$ is the number of divisors of $n$, and for
real $x\geq 1$ put

$$
D_{k}(x)=\sum _{n\leq x}d_{k}(n).
$$

For $\operatorname{Re}(s)>1$ one has $\sum _{n\geq
1}d_{k}(n)n^{-s}=\zeta(s)^{k}$, where $\zeta$ is the Riemann zeta function, and
for $c>1$,

$$
D_{k}(x)={\frac {1}{2\pi i}}\int _{c-i\infty }^{c+i\infty }\zeta ^{k}(w){\frac {x^{w}}{w}}\,dw .
$$

Let $P_{k}$ be the polynomial of degree $k-1$ with real coefficients determined
by

$$
xP_{k}(\log x)=\operatorname*{Res}_{w=1}\;\zeta ^{k}(w){\frac {x^{w}}{w}},
$$

equivalently the unique polynomial of degree
$k-1$ for which $D_{k}(x)-xP_{k}(\log x)=o(x)$ as $x\to \infty$, and define the
error term

$$
\Delta _{k}(x)=D_{k}(x)-xP_{k}(\log x).
$$

For $k=2$ this reads $D_{2}(x)=x\log x+(2\gamma -1)x+\Delta
_{2}(x)$, with $\gamma$ the Euler–Mascheroni constant.

Define

$$
\alpha _{k}=\inf \{\theta \geq 0\;:\;\Delta _{k}(x)=O(x^{\theta })\ \text{as }x\to \infty \},
$$

so that $\alpha _{k}$ is the smallest number for which
$\Delta _{k}(x)=O\!\left(x^{\alpha _{k}+\varepsilon }\right)$ holds for every
$\varepsilon >0$.

Determine the exact value of $\alpha _{k}$ for every integer $k\geq 2$.

title: Hirsch conjecture
literal_statement:
Let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be a
$d$-dimensional convex polytope, i.e. a bounded intersection of finitely many closed half-spaces whose affine hull is $d$-dimensional.
A facet of $P$ is a face of $P$ of dimension
$d-1$, a vertex is a face of dimension $0$, and an edge is a face of dimension
$1$; each edge is incident to exactly two vertices. The graph of $P$ is any
graph whose vertices are in bijection with the vertices of
$P$ in such a way that two vertices of the graph are joined by an edge exactly when the two corresponding vertices of $P$
are the two endpoints of an edge of $P$. Any two graphs of $P$ are isomorphic,
so the diameter

$$
\delta(P) = \max_{u,v} \; \mathrm{dist}(u,v),
$$

the maximum over pairs of vertices of the least number of edges in a path
joining them, is well defined.

For every $d \geq 1$ and every $d$-dimensional convex polytope $P$ with exactly
$n$ facets,

$$
\delta(P) \leq n - d.
$$

title: Conjecture on double-logarithmic diameter and typical distance in preferential attachment graphs
literal_statement:
Let $G_{m,\delta}(t)$ be the preferential attachment graph with parameters $m$ and $\delta$, and let $V_1,V_2\in [t]$ be two uniformly chosen independent vertices. Write $\operatorname{dist}_{G}(V_1,V_2)$ for the graph distance between $V_1$ and $V_2$, and call this the **typical** distance. **Convergence conjecture for $\delta<0$.** Fix $m\geq 2$ and $\delta\in(-m,0)$. Then

$$
\frac{\operatorname{diam}(G_{m,\delta}(t))}{\log\log t}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\operatorname{dist}_{G_{m,\delta}(t)}(V_1,V_2)}{\log\log t}
$$

converge in probability to positive and different constants. The available bounds show double-logarithmic growth of the diameter in this regime, but do not determine the limiting constants or provide a matching lower bound for typical distances.

Source gives growth-order bounds but no typical lower bound. title: Bollobás–Komlós conjecture on embedding bounded-bandwidth graphs
literal_statement: Let $H$ and $G$ be graphs with $|V(H)|=|V(G)|=n$, and write $\bw(H)$ for the band-width of $H$, $\chi(H)$ for its chromatic number, $\Delta(H)$ for its maximum degree, and $\delta(G)$ for the minimum degree of $G$. **Bollobás–Komlós conjecture.** For every $\gamma>0$ and positive integers $r$ and $\Delta$, there is a $\beta>0$ and an $n_0$ such that, whenever $n\ge n_0$, $\chi(H)\le r$, $\Delta(H)\le \Delta$, $\bw(H)<\beta n$, and $\delta(G)\ge (1-1/r+\gamma)n$, then $H$ is a subgraph of $G$. This conjecture proposes a minimum-degree condition guaranteeing the embedding of every bounded-degree, bounded-chromatic graph with sufficiently small band-width.

title: Eventual log-concavity of the coefficients of the q-Catalan numbers
literal_statement:
Let $C_n(q)=\sum_{k=0}^{n(n-1)}m_n(k)q^k$ denote the $q$-Catalan numbers and let $m_n(k)$ be their coefficients. **Log-concavity conjecture.** There exists an integer $t$ such that, when $n$ is sufficiently large, the sequence

$$
\{m_n(t),\ldots,m_n(n(n-1)-t)\}
$$

is log-concave, namely

$$
\left(m_n(k)\right)^2\geq m_n(k+1)m_n(k-1)
$$

for $t+1\leq k\leq n(n-2)-t-1$. Moreover, the minimum value of $t$ seems to be $75$. This is presented as a stronger conjecture suggested by numerical evidence for $n>70$; it remains open.
technical_disposition: Existential fixed t with eventual all-interior log-concavity is stronger than a limiting distribution or unimodality. Source Conjecture 4.2 already contains the t=75 numerical suggestion and unusual n(n-2) index cutoff. Need uniform local coefficient estimates through bulk and boundary; finite polynomial checks cannot prove eventual quantifiers or minimality.

title: Deficiency growth conjecture for Bestvina–Brady approximations
literal_statement:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite flag complex, let $G=G_{\Sigma}$ be the corresponding right-angled Artin group, let $\pi:G\to\mathbf{Z}$ be the canonical surjection, let $H_{\Sigma}=\ker\pi$, and set $\Gamma_n=\pi^{-1}(n\mathbf{Z})$. **Deficiency growth conjecture.** If $\Sigma$ is not simply connected, then

$$
\operatorname{def}(\Gamma_n)\to\infty\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.

title: Linear-edge construction conjecture for sparse intersecting hypergraphs

title: The colliding-permutations conjecture
literal_statement:
Let $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$, and let $\rho(n)$ be the maximum cardinality of a set of pairwise colliding permutations of $[n]$, where two permutations are **colliding** if, viewed as linear orderings, they place two consecutive elements of $[n]$ in the same position. **The colliding-permutations conjecture.** For every $n\in\mathbb{N}$,

$$
\rho(n)={n \choose {\left \lfloor \frac{n}{2} \right \rfloor}}.
$$

The cited previous work established the right-hand side as an upper bound, while the lower bounds available there were substantially smaller; the conjecture is the proposed exact value of the extremal quantity.

Collision means consecutive values at a common coordinate, not shared consecutive patterns. A clique search for one n does not give a uniform construction attaining the bound; closest successor status remains unaudited.
